pts.d: drop the opinion 'I have been harmed', and much of the harm goes with it.

pts.h: Focus only on what is truly yours
pts.d: your choices and character are in your power; reputation, health and fortune are not.

pts.h: Everything passes, so act well now
pts.d: emperors and their mule drivers end the same way; only the present moment is yours.

pts.h: Other people are partners, even when difficult
pts.d: expect rudeness each morning, and answer it with patience instead of anger.

cards.b: Meditations is the private notebook of Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD. He wrote it in Greek, mostly during long military campaigns along the Danube frontier, as a series of notes to himself; its traditional Greek title means simply 'To Himself'. It was never meant for publication. The entries are reminders, arguments and exhortations: how to bear pain, deal with irritating people, face death, resist the corruptions of power and do his duty without complaint. Written by the most powerful man in the world, it is striking for its humility. Marcus is not lecturing others; he is trying, again and again, to persuade himself to live well.

Marcus was a student of Stoicism, a Greek philosophy founded around 300 BC by Zeno of Citium and taught in Marcus's era through the works of the former slave Epictetus. Stoics held that virtue, meaning wisdom, justice, courage and self-control, is the only true good, and that external things, such as wealth, fame, health and even life, are neither good nor bad in themselves. What matters is how we use them. The universe is governed by reason, and humans, sharing in that reason, are fellow citizens of one great community. Meditations is not a treatise that explains these doctrines; it is Marcus's daily practice of applying them to a hard and demanding life.

Marcus did not choose a quiet philosopher's life. Adopted as heir by the emperor Antoninus Pius, he took the throne in 161. His reign was dominated by crises: war with Parthia in the east, a devastating plague, likely smallpox, carried back by returning troops, and years of grinding war against Germanic tribes such as the Marcomanni and Quadi along the Danube. Notes at the end of the first two books of Meditations say they were written 'among the Quadi' and at Carnuntum, a military base near modern Vienna. So these reflections were composed in army camps, by a middle-aged man in poor health, surrounded by death, far from Rome.

The first book of Meditations is a list of debts. Marcus records what he learned from each person who shaped him. From his grandfather, good character and an even temper; from his mother, piety, generosity and simple living; from the Stoic teacher Rusticus, the realization that his character needed correction, and a copy of Epictetus's lectures; from his adoptive father Antoninus Pius, many lessons in patience, steadiness, care for the empire's resources and willingness to listen. It is a moving opening: the emperor begins not with his achievements but with gratitude, and by naming the specific virtues he wants to imitate.

A central Stoic idea, which Marcus inherited from Epictetus, divides everything into two categories. Some things are within our power: our judgments, intentions, desires and actions. Everything else, including our body, property, reputation and what other people do, is ultimately outside our control. Marcus repeatedly reminds himself to put his effort into the first category and accept the second with calm. Suffering comes from treating things outside our control as though our happiness depended on them. This is not passivity; Marcus governed an empire. It means doing one's best, then accepting the outcome, because the outcome was never fully ours to command.

Marcus insists that things themselves cannot touch the mind; our disturbance comes from our own opinions about them. Take away the judgment 'I have been harmed', he writes in effect, and the feeling of harm disappears; take away that feeling, and the harm itself is gone. An insult is just sounds; a loss is an event in the world. What makes them painful is the story we add. Marcus practices describing things plainly, stripped of emotion: a fine dish is a dead fish, a purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. Seeing things as they are takes away their false power over us.

Marcus begins Book Two by telling himself what to expect each day: he will meet meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous and unsociable people. They behave this way because they do not understand what is good and bad. But he does understand, so he cannot be harmed by them, nor can he be angry with them, since they are his kin, sharing the same reason. Humans, he says, were made to work together, like feet, hands, eyelids or the upper and lower rows of teeth. Acting against one another is contrary to nature. Expecting difficulty in advance lets him meet it calmly, rather than being shocked into anger.

Even an emperor struggled to get up. In Book Five, Marcus imagines himself at dawn, reluctant to leave his warm blankets. He argues with himself: was I made to lie under covers and keep warm? Or was I born to do the work of a human being? Plants, birds, ants and bees all do their part in the world's order, and he resists doing his. He notes that people who love their craft wear themselves out for it, forgetting to eat. Should he value his own nature less than an artisan values his trade? The passage is a reminder that duty is not imposed from outside; it is fulfilling what we are.

Marcus returns constantly to impermanence. He imagines the age of the emperor Vespasian: people marrying, raising children, feasting, fighting, flattering and plotting; all of them are gone. Then the age of Trajan: the same, and also gone. Alexander the Great and his mule driver, he notes, ended up in the same place after death. Time is like a river of events, each swept away as soon as it appears. This is not meant to depress him, but to free him. Fame is pointless, because those who remember us will soon be dead too. Anxiety about loss is pointless, because everything changes. What remains is to act rightly now.

Marcus often imagines looking down on human life from a great height. Asia and Europe are corners of the universe; the ocean is a drop; Mount Athos a small clod. He pictures crowds, armies, farms, weddings, births and deaths, all happening at once on a tiny patch of earth in an endless expanse of time. Modern writers call this exercise the view from above. Its purpose is perspective. Our worries and ambitions, which feel enormous, shrink to their real size. Yet Marcus does not conclude that nothing matters. Rather, freed from pettiness, he can focus on what does: acting justly and kindly in the brief time he has.

Marcus describes the mind, when free from passions, as a fortress. There is no stronger refuge, he writes in Book Eight, to which a person can retreat and be safe from capture. The ruling part of the mind, which Stoics called the hegemonikon, cannot be forced by anything outside it; only it can disturb itself. Rather than seeking retreats in the countryside, by the sea or in the mountains, Marcus advises retreating into himself, where calm is available at any moment. He recommends a few short, basic principles kept ready, which can renew the mind and send it back to its work without resentment.

In Book Five, Marcus makes an argument that has become one of the best-known ideas in Meditations. People may obstruct his actions, he writes, but they cannot obstruct his intentions or his character. The mind can adapt, converting any hindrance into a means of pursuing its goal. In this way, what blocks action can itself become the path of action. A rude colleague becomes a chance to practice patience; an illness, a chance to practice courage. Like a fire that consumes whatever is thrown on it and grows brighter, a good mind uses every circumstance as material for virtue, rather than seeing circumstances as reasons to give up.

Anger is one of the passions Marcus works hardest to master. Late in the book he lists reminders for when someone offends him: consider your relationship to them; consider what kind of people they are and what drives them; if they are right, you should not complain; if wrong, they act out of ignorance; you too have done wrong; you cannot be sure they did wrong; life is short; it is not their action that disturbs you, but your judgment of it; anger hurts you more than the offense. Kindness, he concludes, is invincible if it is sincere. He also suggests that the best revenge is to refuse to become like the person who wronged you.

In Book Five, Marcus describes three kinds of people who do a favor. One immediately records it as a debt owed. Another does not demand repayment but privately thinks of the other person as indebted. The third does not even notice what he has done, like a vine that produces grapes and asks nothing more once it has borne its fruit, or a horse that has run its race, or a bee that has made its honey. Having done good, such a person simply moves on to the next good act, as the vine bears grapes again in season. For Marcus, kindness is not a transaction; it is the natural work of a human being.

Marcus knew the dangers of power. In Book Six he warns himself not to be 'Caesarified', not to be soaked in imperial purple and changed by it. He urges himself to stay simple, good, pure, serious, unpretentious, just, devout, kind, affectionate and strong in doing his duty. He holds up his adoptive father, Antoninus Pius, as a model: careful with public money, patient with critics, indifferent to flattery, ready to hear any useful suggestion. For a man with near-absolute authority, these entries are remarkable. They show him using philosophy as a defense against the arrogance, cruelty and self-indulgence that had ruined so many emperors.

In 175, the general Avidius Cassius, governor of Syria and one of Rome's most successful commanders, proclaimed himself emperor after a false rumor that Marcus had died. Marcus prepared to march east. Before he could, Cassius was killed by his own officers after only a few months. According to ancient historians, Marcus regretted losing the chance to show mercy, treated Cassius's family leniently, and had his correspondence destroyed so as not to learn which senators had supported the revolt. Historians treat these reports with some caution, but they fit the forgiving spirit of Meditations, where Marcus repeatedly urges himself to pardon wrongdoers and to assume they act out of ignorance.

Marcus argues that even if you lived three thousand years, or thirty thousand, you could lose only the life you are living now, and you live only the life you are losing. The longest and shortest lives come to the same thing, because the present moment is equal for everyone, and the past and future cannot be taken from us since we do not have them. This leads him to a practical discipline: do each task as if it were the last of your life, without carelessness, pretense or self-pity. Attending fully to the present is how he hopes to live well within the uncertain time remaining.

Marcus thinks about death constantly, not morbidly but as a way of seeing life clearly. Death, he argues, is a natural process like birth, growing teeth, aging or having children. It is simply the dissolution of the elements we are made of, returning them to the cycle of nature. A ripe olive falls, blessing the tree that bore it. Even the great physicians, philosophers and emperors who cured, taught and ruled others have died. Thinking of death should make us neither anxious nor careless, but grateful and serious: it reminds us to stop wasting time and to make each action worthy.

Marcus died in 180, probably at a military camp on the Danube, and was succeeded by his son Commodus, whose cruel and erratic reign many historians see as the start of Rome's long decline. Somehow, his private notebook survived. It was little known for centuries and was first printed in 1559, from a manuscript now lost. Since then it has been read by soldiers, statesmen and ordinary people, and translated into many languages. Its ideas also influenced modern psychology: pioneers of cognitive therapy such as Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck cited the Stoic insight that our interpretations of events, not the events themselves, shape our emotions.

cards.q: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
cards.b: This is the opening of Book Two in George Long's 1862 translation, which is in the public domain. Marcus goes on to explain why none of these people can truly harm him, and why he must not be angry with those who, like him, were made for cooperation.

Some readers find a gap between Marcus's words and his reign. Christians were persecuted under his rule, including the martyrdoms at Lyon in 177, though he did not launch a general campaign. And he made his son Commodus co-emperor and heir, breaking the custom of adopting the best available successor, with disastrous results. Defenders note that Marcus never claimed to be a sage; the book records his struggle to improve, not his success.

As a private notebook, Meditations is repetitive, unsystematic and sometimes gloomy, returning endlessly to death and impermanence. Some critics argue Stoicism can encourage emotional suppression, treating grief and anger as errors rather than natural responses that need expression. Modern Stoics reply that the goal is not to feel nothing but to avoid being ruled by destructive passions. Readers may find it most useful in small doses, as Marcus probably wrote it.

cards.t: Separate the event from your story
cards.b: Marcus describes a purple robe as sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. When something upsets you, write two lines: what actually happened, in plain words, and what you are telling yourself about it. Often the distress lives mostly in the second line, and seeing that is the first step to letting it go.

Each morning Marcus prepared himself to meet difficult people. Take a minute before work to imagine what might go wrong: a rude email, a delay, a frustrating meeting. Decide in advance how you want to respond. When the difficulty arrives, it will feel familiar, and you will have a plan instead of a reflex.

cards.t: Ask: is this up to me?
cards.b: Marcus put his energy only into his own judgments and actions. When you are worried, sort the worry into two columns: what you can do something about and what you cannot. Act on the first column today. For the second, practice letting go. It is not resignation; it is putting effort where it can make a difference.

Marcus argued that a good mind turns obstacles into material for virtue. Next time a plan is blocked, ask what quality this situation lets you practice: patience, creativity, courage or humility. The obstacle may not go away, but your effort can shift from resenting it to growing through it. The question shifts from 'why me?' to 'what now?'

The view from above shrinks our worries to their real size. When something feels overwhelming, picture it from far above: your city, your country, the whole planet and centuries of history. Then ask how much it will matter in five years. Return to the problem with a calmer sense of proportion.

Meditations exists because Marcus wrote his principles down to remind himself. Keep a small notebook of the ideas that steady you, and reread it when you are tired or upset. Writing a principle in your own words, again and again, is how it moves from something you know to something you live.

Marcus asked himself whether he was doing the work of a human being or lying under the blankets. What is the work of a good human being for you today, in your family, your job or your community, and what small, warm blanket is keeping you from it?

cards.b: Richard Thaler, a behavioral economist at the University of Chicago, and Cass Sunstein, a legal scholar then also at Chicago, argue that people often make poor decisions about their health, money and happiness, decisions they would not make if they had full attention, complete information and perfect self-control. Since every choice is presented in some way, the people who design those presentations, whom they call choice architects, inevitably influence what people choose. Rather than pretending to be neutral, choice architects should deliberately design choices to help people make better decisions, as judged by the people themselves. The book offers a toolkit for doing this, from retirement savings to organ donation to the environment.

Thaler and Sunstein propose a political philosophy with a deliberately paradoxical name. It is paternalistic because it tries to influence choices in ways that make people better off. It is libertarian because it insists that people remain free to choose otherwise, ideally at little cost. A nudge, in their definition, is any aspect of choice architecture that predictably changes behavior without forbidding any options or significantly changing economic incentives. Putting fruit at eye level is a nudge; banning junk food is not. The authors believe this approach can appeal across party lines, combining respect for freedom of choice with an evidence-based willingness to help people avoid predictable mistakes.

The book opens with an imaginary friend, Carolyn, who runs food services for a large city school system. Experimenting, she discovers that simply rearranging the food in cafeterias, without changing the menu, can increase or decrease consumption of many items by as much as a quarter. Placing desserts first or last, fruit at eye level or below, fries within easy reach or not, all shift what children eat. What should she do? She could arrange the food to make children healthiest, at random, to maximize profits, or to give children what they would choose on their own. The point is that she cannot avoid choosing an arrangement, and whichever she picks will influence behavior.

Standard economics assumes people are like Homo economicus, an idealized decision maker who thinks like Albert Einstein, stores memory like a supercomputer and has the willpower of Mahatma Gandhi. Thaler and Sunstein call such creatures Econs. Real people, Humans, make predictable errors. Drawing on the work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, the authors describe two systems of thinking: an Automatic System that is fast, intuitive and effortless, and a Reflective System that is slow, deliberate and self-conscious. Much of the time, we run on the Automatic System. Good choice architecture works with that system, making the good choice the easy, obvious one.

Thaler and Sunstein summarize the biases that make nudges necessary. Anchoring: we adjust insufficiently from a starting number. Availability: we judge risks by how easily examples come to mind. Representativeness: we judge by resemblance to stereotypes. Unrealistic optimism: most people think they are above average and less likely than others to suffer misfortune. Loss aversion: losing something hurts about twice as much as gaining it pleases. Status quo bias: we tend to stick with whatever we have. And framing: choices depend on how they are described. Each of these creates opportunities for choice architects to help people, or to exploit them, which is why the authors want to use them responsibly.

At Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport, officials etched the image of a black housefly into each urinal in the men's rooms, near the drain. Men, it turns out, like to aim. According to the managers of the cleaning program, the fly reduced spillage by about 80 percent. The book uses this small, funny example to make a serious point: tiny details of design can have large effects on behavior, often without people noticing. Nobody was ordered to aim better, fined or educated about cleanliness. The fly simply gave the Automatic System a target. Thaler and Sunstein call such small, effective features nudges, and argue that they are everywhere.

A default is what happens if you do nothing. Thaler and Sunstein argue that defaults are among the most powerful nudges because of inertia, status quo bias and the sense that the default is an implicit recommendation. If an employer automatically enrolls workers in a retirement plan unless they opt out, participation is far higher than if workers must take action to opt in. Software settings, phone contracts, magazine subscriptions and insurance plans all have defaults, and they shape what millions of people end up with. Since some default is unavoidable, the authors argue, it should be chosen thoughtfully to serve people's interests, not set carelessly or to benefit the provider.

Thaler and Sunstein describe research by Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein comparing organ donation consent in European countries. Germany and Austria are similar in culture and history. But in Germany, people must explicitly opt in to become organ donors, and only about 12 percent had done so. In Austria, consent is presumed, and people must opt out if they do not want to donate; about 99 percent were donors. The difference came almost entirely from the default. The authors favor a softer approach called mandated choice, in which people are required to state a preference, for example when renewing a driver's license, preserving freedom while overcoming inertia.

Many workers know they should save more for retirement but never get around to it, and raising contributions feels like a pay cut. Thaler and economist Shlomo Benartzi designed a program called Save More Tomorrow. Employees agree in advance to increase their savings rate when they receive future raises. Because the increase comes from future money, it does not feel like a loss; because it is automatic, inertia keeps them enrolled; and participants can quit at any time. In the first company to adopt it, participants' average savings rate rose from about 3.5 percent to over 13 percent in a little over three years. It is a model of a nudge that harnesses biases instead of fighting them.

Humans are easily influenced by what others do and say, and Thaler and Sunstein see this as a powerful lever. They cite classic conformity experiments by Solomon Asch, in which people often gave obviously wrong answers about the length of lines when everyone else in the room did. People want to fit in and assume that others know something they do not. So telling people what most others are doing can change behavior. The authors add a warning: informing people that a bad behavior is common, such as saying many visitors steal petrified wood from a national park, can backfire by making that behavior seem normal. The message should highlight the good behavior of the majority.

In the 1980s, Texas had a serious litter problem on its highways, and appeals to civic duty had little effect on the young men who were most often to blame. The state launched a campaign called Don't Mess with Texas, featuring tough-looking Dallas Cowboys football players and Texas musicians picking up trash and smashing beer cans, with a slogan that tapped into state pride. Within a few years, highway litter had fallen dramatically. In Minnesota, tax officials found something similar: telling taxpayers that most people already paid their taxes in full raised compliance more than threatening them with audits. Social norms, framed well, can do what lectures cannot.

A well-designed system, Thaler and Sunstein argue, expects its users to make mistakes and is as forgiving as possible. Many modern cars beep if you leave your lights on or forget your seatbelt. Some gas tank caps are attached by a strap, so you cannot drive away without them. Many ATMs return your card before giving you cash, because people tend to forget the card once they have what they came for. Engineers call these forcing functions: features that make it hard to proceed without doing the right thing. The authors suggest applying the same thinking to medicine, paperwork and finance, where mistakes are common and costly.

cards.t: The stripes on Lake Shore Drive
cards.b: Lake Shore Drive in Chicago has a dangerous series of S-curves where drivers often went too fast. The city painted white stripes across the road leading into the curve. The stripes start evenly spaced, then get closer together as drivers approach the sharpest part. The narrowing pattern gives drivers the impression that they are speeding up, so they instinctively slow down. Thaler and Sunstein report that, according to the city's traffic engineers, crashes in the following months fell by about a third compared with the same period before. No new signs, fines or police were needed, just a clever use of how the Automatic System perceives speed.

People make better choices when they get clear feedback about what they are doing and understand how options map onto outcomes. Thaler and Sunstein describe an Ambient Orb, a small light that glows red when a household is using a lot of electricity at peak times; owners using it cut peak usage noticeably. Many choices, such as mobile phone plans and credit cards, have deliberately confusing price structures that make comparison hard. The authors propose RECAP, Record, Evaluate and Compare Alternative Prices, a rule requiring sellers to disclose fees and usage clearly, ideally in machine-readable form, so that customers or websites can compare plans and see what they actually pay.

In 2000, Sweden reformed its pension system, allowing workers to choose how to invest part of their retirement savings from among 456 funds. The government encouraged active choice through an advertising campaign, and one fund was designated as a carefully designed default for those who did not choose. Two-thirds of workers made an active choice that first year. Thaler and Sunstein report the results were not encouraging: people who chose actively tended to pick funds with higher fees, invest heavily in Swedish stocks and chase recent performance, especially technology stocks just before they crashed. The default fund did better. The lesson: when choices are complex, a good default and structured help matter more than more options.

When choices are simple, people can compare every option carefully. When there are many options with many features, they switch to simplifying strategies, such as eliminating any option that fails one criterion. Thaler and Sunstein call this situation the problem of complex choices and argue that choice architects should help by organizing options. Paint stores group colors by shade and show samples rather than listing names; a good guide to mutual funds might sort them by risk and fees. The authors also argue for collaborative filtering, the recommendations based on people like you used by online stores, as a way to make sense of huge numbers of options.

Thaler and Sunstein recognize that nudges could be used manipulatively. Their test, adapted from the philosopher John Rawls, is the publicity principle: a government should not adopt a policy that it would be unwilling or unable to defend publicly to its own citizens. A nudge that works only if people do not know about it, like subliminal advertising, fails the test. Defaults, reminders and clear information pass. The authors also urge choice architects to make opting out easy and to nudge people toward outcomes they would choose for themselves. They acknowledge the risk of a slippery slope, but argue that since choice architecture is unavoidable, the real question is how to do it well.

Thaler and Sunstein argue that nudges can help the environment, and their favorite example is a law that simply required information. In 1986 the United States Congress passed a law creating the Toxic Release Inventory, which required companies to report publicly the quantities of hazardous chemicals they stored and released. The law did not ban anything or impose new taxes. Yet once the numbers became public, environmental groups and the media publicized the worst polluters, and companies, eager to avoid being named on such lists, cut their releases substantially. The authors see this as a model: making behavior visible, through feedback and disclosure, can achieve results without heavy regulation.

cards.q: There is no such thing as a neutral design: whatever you do, you are influencing people's choices.
cards.b: This is a paraphrase of a central claim of Nudge, not the authors' exact words. It is the book's answer to critics who say governments and companies should not nudge: they already do, whether they intend to or not.

cards.t: Smaller effects in the real world
cards.b: Nudge inspired governments to create behavioral insights units, including Britain's 'Nudge Unit' in 2010, and Thaler won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2017. But later research found that many nudges have smaller effects than early studies suggested. A 2022 study by Stefano DellaVigna and Elizabeth Linos found that nudges tested by government units at scale had average effects far smaller than those reported in academic papers. Some meta-analyses also found signs of publication bias. Defaults remain strong; many other nudges are modest.

Critics from both left and right object to nudging. Some argue that steering people's choices through their biases, even for good ends, disrespects their autonomy and can slide into manipulation. Others argue that nudges are a distraction from tougher measures, such as taxes, regulation or structural reform, which may be needed for problems like climate change or poverty. Sunstein has responded with further books defending nudges as complements to, not substitutes for, other policies.

Save More Tomorrow shows the power of automatic choices. Use defaults on yourself: set up automatic transfers to savings on payday, schedule recurring medical checkups, and pre-commit to future increases. Make the good choice the one that happens when you do nothing, so inertia works for you rather than against you.

Carolyn found that the order of food changed what children ate. Your kitchen, desk and phone are your cafeteria. Put healthy food at eye level, move tempting apps off your home screen and keep important tools within easy reach. Small changes in layout can shift your habits more than willpower alone.

ATMs return your card before your cash because people forget. Look for repeated mistakes in your life or work, such as forgotten keys, missed deadlines or wrong attachments, and design a forcing function: a hook by the door, an automatic calendar reminder, a checklist before sending. Assume you will err and make the error hard.

cards.t: Use the norm, not the problem
cards.b: The petrified wood and Minnesota tax examples show that describing bad behavior as common can backfire, while highlighting the good majority helps. When encouraging your team or family to change, emphasize how many people already do the right thing, rather than complaining about how many do not. A positive norm invites people to join; a negative one gives them permission to misbehave.

Thaler and Sunstein say a good nudge is one you could defend openly. When you design choices for others, as a parent, manager or marketer, ask whether you would be comfortable explaining exactly what you did and why. If the answer is no, you have probably crossed from helping into manipulating.

Swedish workers given 456 funds often chose badly. When facing a complex choice, like a pension, a phone plan or health insurance, narrow the options first using a few key criteria, such as fees and risk. A good default or a trusted, simple guide is often better than trying to evaluate every possible option yourself.

Thaler and Sunstein say we are all choice architects for someone. Whose choices do you shape, at home, at work or online, and how? If you redesigned one of those choices to make the better option easier, what would you change?

label: Book 16
title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
subtitle: Powerful Lessons in Personal Change
author: Stephen R. Covey

cards.b: If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Character matters more than technique
pts.d: lasting effectiveness comes from principles, not quick-fix personality tricks.

pts.h: Between stimulus and response lies your freedom
pts.d: proactive people focus on their circle of influence instead of blaming circumstances.

pts.h: Spend time on the important, not just the urgent
pts.d: Quadrant II work, like planning and relationships, prevents tomorrow's crises.

pts.h: Understand first, then be understood
pts.d: empathic listening and win-win thinking turn conflict into synergy.

cards.b: Stephen Covey, a teacher of leadership and organizational behavior, studied two hundred years of American writing on success and noticed a shift. Older literature emphasized the Character Ethic: integrity, humility, courage, patience, the Golden Rule. After the First World War, it emphasized the Personality Ethic: image, attitudes, techniques and quick fixes for influencing people. Covey argues that real, lasting effectiveness comes from character based on universal principles, and that techniques without character are manipulative and fragile. He presents seven habits, each a combination of knowledge, skill and desire, that move people from dependence to independence and finally to interdependence, the ability to work effectively with others.

Covey's approach is inside-out: change begins with yourself, your paradigms, character and motives, before you try to change others or circumstances. He describes a maturity continuum. Dependent people rely on others and blame them: you take care of me, you did this to me. Independent people take responsibility: I can do it, I am responsible. Interdependent people go further: we can cooperate and combine our talents to achieve more. The first three habits, the private victory, build independence. The next three, the public victory, build interdependence. The seventh habit renews all the others. Covey insists the order matters: you cannot have public victories without private ones.

Covey describes a time when one of his sons was struggling at school and in sports, awkward and socially immature. Covey and his wife Sandra tried everything to help: encouragement, coaching, positive thinking. Nothing worked. Then they realized that their deepest message to him, beneath all the techniques, was that he was not capable and needed protecting. They decided to change their own way of seeing him, to relax, enjoy him and stop comparing him to others. Over time, their son began to blossom, becoming outstanding socially, academically and athletically. Covey calls this a paradigm shift: changing how we see a situation changes how we behave and what results follow.

One Sunday morning on a New York subway, Covey recounts, passengers were sitting quietly until a man boarded with his children, who began yelling, throwing things and grabbing people's papers. The father sat with his eyes closed, doing nothing. Irritated, Covey finally asked him if he could control his children. The man looked up and said, softly, that they had just come from the hospital, where the children's mother had died about an hour ago. He did not know what to think, and he supposed they did not either. Instantly, Covey writes, his irritation vanished and was replaced by compassion. Nothing in the situation had changed except his paradigm.

A paradigm, in Covey's use, is the way we see the world: the mental map by which we understand, interpret and evaluate. Our behavior flows from our paradigms, so changing behavior without changing paradigms rarely lasts. But maps can be wrong. Covey argues that the best maps align with principles, natural laws of human interaction such as fairness, integrity, honesty, service and growth. He illustrates with a story of a battleship captain who, seeing a light ahead in fog, signaled the other vessel to change course. The reply came back that it should change course. The captain insisted, announcing his rank. The final reply: 'I'm a lighthouse.' Principles do not move.

cards.t: The goose and the golden eggs
cards.b: Covey uses Aesop's fable of a farmer whose goose laid a golden egg each day. Greedy and impatient, the farmer killed the goose to get all the eggs at once and found none. Covey's lesson is the P/PC Balance: effectiveness requires balancing P, production of desired results, with PC, production capability, the asset or ability that produces them. A person who works without sleep or exercise, a manager who drives employees too hard, or a parent who wins arguments by force are all killing their geese. Covey applies this to physical assets, finances, human relationships and our own health and skills. Caring for capability is what sustains results.

The first habit is about responsibility, which Covey reads as response-ability: the ability to choose your response. Drawing on Viktor Frankl, he argues that between stimulus and response, human beings have the freedom to choose. Reactive people are driven by feelings, circumstances and conditions; their language shows it: 'There's nothing I can do', 'He makes me so mad', 'I have to'. Proactive people are driven by values; they say 'Let's look at alternatives', 'I control my feelings', 'I choose'. Covey argues that love, for example, is a verb, an action you can choose, not just a feeling that comes and goes. Proactivity is the foundation for all the other habits.

cards.t: Circle of concern, circle of influence
cards.b: Covey asks readers to picture two circles. The circle of concern contains everything we care about: our health, children, work, national debt, nuclear war. Inside it, a smaller circle of influence contains what we can actually do something about. Reactive people focus on the circle of concern, on the weaknesses of others and problems they cannot control, and their circle of influence shrinks. Proactive people focus on the circle of influence, working on things they can change, and that circle expands. Covey suggests a simple test: listen to whether you talk in terms of 'have', as in 'if only I had a better boss', or 'be', as in 'I can be more patient'.

cards.t: Habit 2: Begin with the end in mind
cards.b: The second habit rests on the principle that all things are created twice: first in the mind, then in reality. A building starts with a blueprint, a trip with a destination. If you do not consciously design your own first creation, Covey says, other people and circumstances will design it for you. He urges readers to write a personal mission statement, a kind of personal constitution setting out what they want to be, what they want to do, and the values and principles behind both. Covey distinguishes leadership, which asks whether we are doing the right things, from management, which asks how to do things well. It does no good to climb efficiently if the ladder leans on the wrong wall.

Covey asks readers to imagine driving to a funeral, walking into the room and seeing friends and family gathered. Then they realize it is their own funeral, three years from now. Four speakers will talk about them: a family member, a friend, a colleague from work, and someone from their church or community organization. What would you want each of them to say about your character, contributions and achievements? What difference would you want to have made in their lives? Covey says that if you take the exercise seriously, you will touch some of your deepest values. It is a practical way to begin with the end in mind.

Habit 3 is the practice of Habit 2: managing yourself according to your priorities. Covey offers a time management matrix with two dimensions: urgent and important. Quadrant I holds urgent and important tasks, such as crises and deadlines. Quadrant II holds important but not urgent tasks: planning, prevention, relationship-building, exercise, learning. Quadrant III holds urgent but unimportant interruptions, many meetings and phone calls. Quadrant IV holds trivial time-wasters. Effective people, Covey argues, spend as much time as possible in Quadrant II, saying no to Quadrants III and IV. Because Quadrant II work prevents problems, over time it shrinks Quadrant I, reducing the crises that dominate many lives.

To show effective delegation, Covey tells how he taught his seven-year-old son Stephen to care for the family lawn. Rather than give step-by-step orders, he showed his son two yards, one green and clean, and the neighbor's, and agreed on the result they wanted. Stephen could do it however he liked, and they would walk the yard together twice a week so he could judge his own work. For days, Stephen did nothing; the lawn yellowed and litter piled up. Covey held back and asked how it was going. Stephen burst into tears, then asked for help, and from that day kept the yard green and clean. Covey calls this stewardship delegation: focusing on results, not methods.

Before the public victory habits, Covey introduces a metaphor for trust: the emotional bank account. We make deposits in relationships through courtesy, kindness, honesty and keeping commitments, and withdrawals through discourtesy, disrespect, overreaction and broken promises. When the account is high, communication is easy, and even mistakes are forgiven. When it is overdrawn, every word is suspect. Covey lists six major deposits: understanding the individual, attending to little things, keeping commitments, clarifying expectations, showing personal integrity, and apologizing sincerely when you make a withdrawal. He stresses that what counts as a deposit depends on the other person, so you must understand them first.

Covey describes six paradigms of human interaction: win-win, win-lose, lose-win, lose-lose, win, and win-win or no deal. Win-win is a frame of mind that seeks mutual benefit in all interactions. It is based on an abundance mentality, the belief that there is plenty for everyone, rather than a scarcity mentality that sees life as a fixed pie. Covey recommends making win-win or no deal an option: if two parties cannot find a solution that benefits both, they agree to disagree agreeably and do not make a deal. Having that option frees people from pressure to manipulate or give in, and makes it easier to look for genuinely shared solutions.

To introduce Habit 5, Covey imagines visiting an optometrist and complaining about your eyesight. After barely listening, the optometrist takes off his own glasses and hands them to you, saying he has worn them for ten years and they have done wonders for him, so you should take them. You put them on and see even worse. He tells you to try harder and think positively. Would you go back to that optometrist? Covey points out that we often do exactly this in conversation: we diagnose and prescribe before we understand. In relationships, at work and at home, we give advice from our own experience before seeing the other person's situation.

Covey calls Habit 5 the most important principle in interpersonal relations: seek first to understand, then to be understood. Most people listen with the intent to reply, filtering everything through their own autobiography. They evaluate, probe, advise or interpret. Covey urges empathic listening instead: listening with the intent to understand, getting inside another person's frame of reference, and reflecting back both the content and the feelings of what they say. This is not agreeing; it is deeply understanding. Only after someone feels understood, Covey argues, are they open to influence. The second half of the habit is presenting your own view clearly, logically and in a way that addresses their concerns.

Synergy means the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. In relationships and teams, it arises when people with different perspectives respect their differences and work together creatively to find a third alternative better than what either proposed. Covey describes a couple disagreeing about a vacation: one wants a long-planned fishing trip, the other wants to visit a sick parent. Rather than one winning or both compromising, real communication might uncover a new plan that serves both deeper needs. Synergy is risky, because it means being open to an outcome you cannot predict. But it is built on the trust and understanding of the earlier habits, and it is the reward of interdependence.

Covey tells of a man in the woods working feverishly to saw down a tree. He has been at it for over five hours and is exhausted, but making slow progress. A passer-by suggests he take a few minutes to sharpen the saw, which would make the work go much faster. The man replies that he does not have time to sharpen the saw; he is too busy sawing. Covey uses this story to introduce Habit 7: taking time to renew yourself is not a distraction from your work. It is what makes the work possible, and neglecting it, however busy you are, guarantees declining results over time.

Habit 7 is preserving and enhancing your greatest asset: yourself. Covey identifies four dimensions of renewal. Physical: exercise, nutrition and rest. Spiritual: values, reflection, prayer, nature, great literature or music. Mental: reading, writing, learning and planning. Social and emotional: service, empathy and deep relationships. These are Quadrant II activities, important but never urgent, so they are easy to neglect. Covey recommends spending about an hour a day on the first three, which he calls the daily private victory. Renewal across all four dimensions, he argues, creates an upward spiral of growth, letting each of the other habits work at a higher level.

cards.q: Between what happens to us and how we respond lies a space, and in that space is our freedom to choose.
cards.b: This is a paraphrase of an idea Covey draws from Viktor Frankl, not his exact words. It is the foundation of Habit 1: we cannot control everything that happens to us, but we can choose our response, and that choice shapes who we become.

The 7 Habits has sold tens of millions of copies and is widely used in business training, but critics note that its evidence is mostly anecdotal: stories from Covey's family, consulting work and teaching. Covey presents his principles as universal and self-evident, yet offers little research to show that the habits cause effectiveness. Much of the advice, such as listening well and planning ahead, is sensible, but its packaging as a complete system can overstate how much it has been tested.

cards.t: Borrowed ideas and a moral frame
cards.b: Some reviewers observe that many ideas in the book are adapted from others: the urgent-important matrix is associated with President Eisenhower, the stimulus-response gap with Viktor Frankl, and much of the habit language with older self-help. Others find Covey's tone preachy, and note that his principles reflect his own religious and cultural values more than he acknowledges. Readers can still benefit, while recognizing that the habits are one useful framework rather than natural laws.

cards.t: Swap reactive words for proactive ones
cards.b: Covey showed that our language reveals whether we are reactive or proactive. For a day, notice when you say 'I have to', 'There's nothing I can do' or 'She makes me angry'. Replace them with 'I choose to', 'Let's look at alternatives' and 'I feel angry and I can decide what to do'. The shift in words gradually shifts how you act.

The funeral exercise reveals what you really value. Take twenty minutes to write what you hope a family member, a friend, a colleague and a community member would say about you. Compare it with how you spent last week. Then pick one specific change that would bring your daily life closer to the person you described.

Important but non-urgent work, like planning, exercise and building relationships, always loses to urgent demands unless you protect it. At the start of each week, block time in your calendar for your most important Quadrant II activities before anything else. Treat these appointments with yourself as seriously as a meeting with your boss.

The optometrist who handed over his own glasses never understood the patient. In your next difficult conversation, resist the urge to advise or argue. Reflect back what the other person is saying and feeling until they confirm you have it right. Only then share your view. You may find that the conflict shrinks once people feel heard.

The emotional bank account fills through small, consistent acts. Choose one important relationship and plan a deposit this week: keep a promise you have postponed, do a small kindness, apologize for something you have let slide. Trust built this way gives you room for honest conversations and forgiveness when mistakes happen.

Covey's 'green and clean' agreement with his son focused on the outcome and let the child decide how to achieve it. When you hand off a task, at work or at home, describe clearly what success looks like, agree on how it will be checked, and then step back. People grow and take ownership when they are trusted with the how.

Covey asks what one thing you could do regularly, that you are not doing now, which would make a tremendous positive difference in your personal life, and one thing for your work. What are those two things for you, and what is stopping you from starting this week?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Imagination drove Einstein's science
pts.d: thought experiments, like chasing a light beam, led him to relativity.

pts.h: Rebelliousness fueled his creativity
pts.d: his distrust of authority let him question absolute time when others would not.

pts.h: He changed physics while working outside the academy
pts.d: his 1905 miracle year came from a junior clerk at the Bern patent office.

pts.h: The rebel became a conservative about quantum theory
pts.d: he spent decades resisting randomness and seeking a unified theory he never found.

cards.b: Walter Isaacson's biography follows Albert Einstein from his birth in Ulm, Germany, in 1879 to his death in Princeton in 1955. Using Einstein's personal letters, many released only in 2006, Isaacson shows the man behind the icon: a brilliant, playful, stubborn and sometimes cold person who transformed our understanding of space, time, light and gravity. The book explains his science in accessible terms, but its central interest is how Einstein thought. Isaacson argues that his genius lay not only in mathematical skill, which others surpassed, but in imagination, a willingness to question accepted wisdom, and a deep faith that nature's laws are simple and harmonious.

Isaacson draws a thread between Einstein's science and his character. His creativity flowed from a rebellious, nonconformist streak: he disliked rote learning, mocked pompous authority and refused to accept ideas simply because they were traditional. This made him a pioneer of relativity, which overturned centuries of thinking about space and time. The same independence shaped his politics: he defended individual freedom, opposed nationalism and militarism, and spoke out against racism. Isaacson also notes a paradox: the young rebel later became a stubborn defender of classical certainty against quantum mechanics. The book asks what we can learn from both his imaginative daring and his blind spots.

When Einstein was about five and sick in bed, his father showed him a compass. The boy was amazed that the needle always pointed north, as if moved by an invisible force, even though nothing touched it. He later said the experience made a deep and lasting impression and taught him that something deeply hidden had to be behind things. Isaacson treats this as an early sign of Einstein's lifelong sense of wonder about invisible forces and fields. He was a slow talker as a child, and family stories said he repeated sentences softly to himself before speaking. But he was intensely curious, persistent and capable of long concentration.

Einstein hated the rigid, militaristic teaching at his Munich school, the Luitpold Gymnasium, where students were expected to memorize and obey. A teacher once told him that his presence in class undermined respect. At fifteen, he left without graduating and joined his family in Italy. He then attended a progressive school in Aarau, Switzerland, which encouraged independent thinking and visual imagination. There, at sixteen, he first pictured what it would be like to ride alongside a beam of light. If he moved at light's speed, would he see a frozen wave? Something seemed wrong with that picture, and the puzzle would lead him to special relativity a decade later.

Einstein studied physics at the Zurich Polytechnic, where he often skipped lectures and annoyed professors, one of whom called him a clever boy who would never let anyone tell him anything. After graduating in 1900 he could not get an academic job. In 1902, with help from a friend's father, he became a technical expert, third class, at the Swiss patent office in Bern. The job turned out to be a blessing. Evaluating inventions, many involving electrical signals and synchronized clocks, sharpened his thinking. With friends he formed the Olympia Academy, a small discussion club that read philosophy and science. Free of academic pressure, he thought about physics in his spare time.

In 1905, at twenty-six, while working six days a week at the patent office, Einstein published four papers that changed physics. In March, he proposed that light could behave as particles, or quanta, explaining the photoelectric effect. In May, he showed that the jiggling of particles in liquid, called Brownian motion, proved atoms exist and let their size be calculated. In June, he introduced special relativity, abolishing absolute time and space. In September, he derived the equivalence of mass and energy, E equals mc squared. He also completed a doctoral dissertation. Isaacson calls it the most astonishing creative burst in the history of science since Newton's plague year of 1666.

Isaacson explains special relativity through its two starting assumptions: the laws of physics are the same for all observers moving at constant speed, and the speed of light is the same for all of them. Holding both firmly forces strange conclusions. A clock moving relative to you ticks more slowly, a phenomenon called time dilation. A moving object is shortened in its direction of motion. Two events simultaneous for one observer may not be for another. These effects are tiny at everyday speeds, which is why we never notice them, but they become large near the speed of light. Isaacson emphasizes that Einstein's leap was not new mathematics but the courage to abandon absolute time.

Isaacson stresses Einstein's distinctive way of thinking: visual, imaginative thought experiments, or Gedankenexperimente. He pictured trains and lightning strikes, people in falling elevators, and riders on beams of light, then asked what observers would see. In one, lightning strikes both ends of a moving train at what an observer on the platform judges to be the same moment; a passenger in the middle of the train sees one flash first. Simultaneity, Einstein realized, depends on your frame of reference. Isaacson links this skill to the Swiss school's visual teaching and the patent office's concrete puzzles. Einstein himself said imagination mattered more than knowledge, because knowledge is limited.

In 1907, sitting at his desk at the patent office, Einstein had what he later called the happiest thought of his life. A person falling freely from a roof would not feel their own weight. Gravity and acceleration, he realized, are equivalent: there is no experiment inside a closed elevator that could tell whether you were at rest in a gravitational field or accelerating through empty space. This principle of equivalence started him on an eight-year struggle to generalize relativity to include gravity. He had to master difficult new mathematics with the help of his friend Marcel Grossmann, and he made several false starts along the way.

By November 1915, Einstein was in Berlin, exhausted, separated from his family and racing the great mathematician David Hilbert, who was also working on gravitational field equations. Over four consecutive weeks, Einstein presented papers to the Prussian Academy, revising his equations each time. He then tested the theory on a known puzzle: the orbit of Mercury shifts slightly more than Newton's laws predict. His equations gave exactly the right amount. He later said the result gave him heart palpitations. General relativity described gravity as the curvature of spacetime by mass and energy. Isaacson presents the tangled priority question with Hilbert carefully, concluding that Einstein deserves credit for the theory.

General relativity predicted that the sun's gravity would bend starlight by a specific amount. In 1919, British expeditions led by Arthur Eddington photographed stars during a solar eclipse and reported that the light was deflected as Einstein predicted. At a joint meeting of the Royal Society and Royal Astronomical Society in London that November, the result was announced, and newspapers around the world proclaimed a revolution in science. Einstein, previously known mainly to physicists, became the world's first scientific celebrity. Isaacson explains that the timing helped: after the horror of the First World War, a German scientist confirmed by British astronomers seemed to symbolize international reconciliation.

Isaacson does not hide Einstein's personal failings. He married Mileva Marić, a fellow physics student, in 1903; before the marriage they had a daughter, Lieserl, whose fate remains unknown. They had two sons, Hans Albert and Eduard, who later developed schizophrenia. As the marriage collapsed, Einstein drew up a cold list of conditions Mileva must accept to keep living with him. In their divorce settlement he promised her the money from a Nobel Prize he had not yet won, and kept the promise when it came. He then married his cousin Elsa. Letters show he could be warm and playful, but also detached, and he often put his work before his family.

Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded in 1922, not for relativity, which the committee still regarded as controversial, but for his law of the photoelectric effect. Ironically, that 1905 insight about light quanta helped launch quantum mechanics, a theory he would come to resist. In the 1920s, physicists such as Niels Bohr and Werner Heisenberg developed quantum theory, which describes nature in terms of probabilities and uncertainty. Einstein accepted that the theory worked, but believed it was incomplete. He insisted that reality must exist independently of observation and follow strict causal laws. He famously remarked that he was convinced God did not play dice.

At the Solvay conferences in Brussels in 1927 and 1930, Einstein challenged Niels Bohr with ingenious thought experiments meant to show that quantum uncertainty could be beaten. Each morning, Einstein would present a new puzzle at breakfast; by evening, Bohr would usually have found the flaw. In 1930, Einstein proposed a box releasing a single photon on a timer, to measure energy and time precisely together. After a sleepless night, Bohr showed that Einstein had forgotten the effect of his own general relativity on the clock. Isaacson presents these debates as among the greatest in the history of science, conducted with deep mutual respect.

Isaacson highlights a striking irony. The young Einstein had overturned Newtonian absolutes, trusting his intuition against established authority. The older Einstein refused to accept quantum mechanics as complete, trusting his intuition that nature was deterministic and real, against the new consensus. From the 1920s until his death, he spent most of his energy seeking a unified field theory that would combine gravity and electromagnetism and, he hoped, restore certainty. He never found it, and many younger physicists saw him as out of touch. Yet Isaacson notes that his objections, especially the 1935 paper on what is now called entanglement, raised questions that remain central in physics today.

As a famous Jewish scientist and a pacifist in Berlin, Einstein became a target of nationalist and antisemitic attacks in the 1920s; some critics denounced relativity as 'Jewish physics'. When Hitler came to power in January 1933, Einstein was visiting the United States. He announced he would not return to Germany, renounced his German citizenship and resigned from the Prussian Academy. Nazi authorities seized his property. He settled at the new Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, where he remained for the rest of his life. He used his fame to help many other Jewish refugees, writing affidavits and letters to help them reach safety.

In August 1939, the Hungarian physicist Leo Szilard, worried that Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb, persuaded Einstein to sign a letter to President Franklin Roosevelt. It warned that a nuclear chain reaction in uranium could lead to extremely powerful bombs and urged American research. The letter helped prompt early government interest, though the Manhattan Project developed later and Einstein, considered a security risk, was not involved. After Hiroshima, he regretted signing it, saying that had he known the Germans would fail, he would have done nothing. He spent his final years campaigning for nuclear arms control and a world government to prevent war.

Einstein's politics, Isaacson argues, flowed from his love of individual freedom. He opposed authoritarianism, defended free speech during the McCarthy era and spoke out against American racism, calling segregation a disease of white people, not of Black people. In 1937, when the singer Marian Anderson was refused a room at a Princeton hotel, he invited her to stay at his home. In 1952 he was offered the presidency of Israel and declined. On religion, Einstein rejected a personal God who rewards and punishes, but described himself as deeply religious in another sense: filled with awe at the order and harmony of the universe. He often cited the philosopher Spinoza's God, revealed in nature's lawful harmony.

In April 1955, Einstein suffered a ruptured aortic aneurysm. He refused surgery, saying he wanted to go when he wanted and that it was tasteless to prolong life artificially. In the hospital, he asked for his notes and continued working on his unified field theory. He died early on April 18, aged 76, leaving pages of equations by his bed. During the autopsy, the pathologist Thomas Harvey removed his brain without clear permission and kept it for decades, hoping to discover the secret of his genius. Isaacson notes that the brain revealed little, and that Einstein's genius lay in his imagination, persistence and willingness to wonder.

cards.q: Imagination matters more than knowledge, because knowledge is limited to what we now understand.
cards.b: This is a paraphrase of one of Einstein's best-known remarks, which Isaacson uses to explain his thinking, not his exact words. It captures why thought experiments, not just calculations, were at the heart of his discoveries.

cards.t: Science made simple, maybe too simple
cards.b: Reviewers praised Isaacson's clear explanations, but some physicists felt that the science chapters simplify complex ideas, especially quantum theory and the unified field theory, to the point of losing nuance. Others noted that, as a journalist rather than a historian of science, Isaacson relies heavily on the work of scholars on the Einstein Papers Project. The book is best read as an accessible portrait, with specialist histories available for deeper detail.

Some readers felt Isaacson treats Einstein's treatment of Mileva and his sons too gently, explaining it in the context of his time and genius rather than judging it fully. Others argue the opposite, that the book's use of private letters gives a candid view of his flaws. The question of Mileva's possible contributions to his early work is discussed, and Isaacson concludes the evidence is weak; some scholars disagree.

Einstein discovered relativity by imagining himself riding a light beam. When facing a hard problem at work or in life, try picturing it concretely: walk through the scenario step by step, imagine extreme cases, and ask what you would actually see. Vivid imagination can reveal contradictions that abstract analysis misses.

Einstein did his greatest work as a patent clerk, thinking in his spare hours, away from academic pressures. Find time in your week that is free from obligations and distractions, even an hour, and use it to think about problems that fascinate you. Some of the most valuable work happens outside official roles.

The young Einstein defied the experts and was right; the old Einstein defied a new consensus and was mostly wrong. Challenge received wisdom, but also challenge your own long-held convictions. Ask regularly whether you are holding a view because of evidence or because it is yours, as Einstein found with quantum mechanics.

Einstein never lost the wonder he felt at a compass needle as a five-year-old. Notice small mysteries around you, such as why the sky is blue or how your phone finds its location, and look into them. Curiosity is a habit that grows with use, and it keeps learning alive throughout life.

cards.t: Don't let work crowd out people
cards.b: Einstein's single-minded focus produced great science but damaged his family relationships. Ask whether your commitment to work is costing the people closest to you more than you realize. Set aside protected time for family and friends, and treat those relationships as part of a well-lived life, not an interruption to it.

Einstein used his fame to rescue refugees, oppose racism and call for nuclear arms control. Whatever influence you have, at work, in your community or online, consider how you might use it to help someone with less. Speaking up, writing a letter or opening your home, as Einstein did for Marian Anderson, can matter enormously.

Einstein said he had no special talents, only passionate curiosity. What question fascinates you that you have never given yourself time to explore? What would it take to spend an hour on it this week, simply for the joy of understanding?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Beliefs about ability shape how you handle challenge
pts.d: a fixed mindset avoids difficulty; a growth mindset seeks it out to learn.

pts.h: Praise effort and strategy, not intelligence
pts.d: children praised for being smart started avoiding hard puzzles and even lied about scores.

pts.h: Failure means 'not yet', not 'not able'
pts.d: in a growth mindset, setbacks are information rather than verdicts on who you are.

pts.h: Mindsets can change, but not by slogans
pts.d: noticing your fixed-mindset voice and choosing to learn is the real work.

cards.b: Carol Dweck, a psychologist at Stanford University, spent decades studying why some people thrive on challenges while others crumble at the first setback. Her answer is a simple idea with large consequences: people hold different beliefs, or mindsets, about the nature of ability. In a fixed mindset, you believe your intelligence, talents and personality are carved in stone, so every task becomes a test of how much you have. In a growth mindset, you believe basic qualities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others. Dweck argues that these beliefs shape how people approach learning, sport, business, relationships and parenting, often more than raw talent does.

Dweck's point is not that everyone can become Einstein or that anyone can do anything. It is that people's true potential is unknown and unknowable, and that believing ability is fixed creates an urgency to prove yourself over and over. Every situation becomes a judgment: will I look smart or dumb, succeed or fail, be accepted or rejected? People in a growth mindset ask instead: what can I learn here? Dweck traces how this difference leads one group to avoid challenges, give up easily and feel threatened by others' success, while the other embraces challenges, persists and finds inspiration in others. The rest of the book shows the pattern in many areas of life.

cards.t: The boy who loved a challenge
cards.b: Early in her career, Dweck gave children a series of puzzles that grew progressively harder, expecting to study how they coped with failure. Some children were upset and discouraged. But others surprised her. One ten-year-old boy pulled up his chair, rubbed his hands together and declared that he loved a challenge. Another, sweating over a puzzle, said happily that he had hoped it would be informative. Dweck realized these children did not even think they were failing; they thought they were learning. This changed her research. She stopped asking simply how people cope with failure, and began asking what makes some people see difficulty as an opportunity.

In the fixed mindset, Dweck explains, ability is a fixed amount, and its owner feels compelled to prove it. Success means you are smart or talented; failure means you are not. Effort is suspect, because if you were really gifted you would not need to try hard. This produces predictable behavior. People avoid challenges in which they might fail, prefer tasks they know they can do, give up quickly when things get hard, ignore useful criticism and feel threatened by others' success. Dweck notes that the fixed mindset can feel comforting, because it offers a simple sense of identity. But it limits growth, because learning always involves looking clumsy for a while.

In the growth mindset, Dweck writes, the hand you are dealt is just the starting point. Abilities can be cultivated through effort, strategy, practice and help from others. This does not mean believing everyone is equal or that anyone can become anything; it means believing that people can grow. In this mindset, challenges are interesting, effort is the path to mastery, criticism is useful information and other people's success is a source of lessons. Failure still hurts, but it does not define you; it tells you what to work on. Dweck stresses that people are often a mix of the two mindsets and can hold different mindsets in different areas.

In a study with Claudia Mueller, Dweck gave hundreds of fifth-graders a set of fairly easy puzzles. Afterward, some were praised for their intelligence, 'You must be smart at this', and others for their effort, 'You must have worked hard'. When offered a choice of next task, most children praised for intelligence chose an easy one, while most praised for effort chose a challenging one they could learn from. When all were then given very hard problems, the intelligence-praised children enjoyed them less and later performed worse. When asked to write their scores for another school, about 40 percent of the intelligence-praised children exaggerated them. Praising ability, Dweck concludes, pushed children into a fixed mindset.

Dweck describes a study at Columbia University in which people answered difficult general-knowledge questions while their brain activity was monitored. After each answer, they were told whether they were right, then given the correct answer. People with a fixed mindset showed strong brain activity when told whether they were right or wrong, but paid little attention when shown the correct information. People with a growth mindset paid close attention to the information that could help them learn. Later, when retested, those who had attended to the learning information did better. Dweck uses this to show that mindset shapes what people notice: their status, or their chance to improve.

Dweck contrasts sports stars. John McEnroe, the tennis champion, was supremely talented but, in her reading, had a fixed mindset: he blamed losses on others, on line judges, fans and conditions, and did not love learning. Michael Jordan, by contrast, was not seen as a natural early on. He was left off his high school varsity team and was passed over by some college and NBA teams. He responded by practicing relentlessly, working on weaknesses, and treating failure as motivation. Even at his peak, he was known for working harder than anyone else. Dweck argues that, in sport, the idea of 'naturals' can blind both athletes and coaches to the role of persistence.

Dweck describes Wilma Rudolph, born prematurely in Tennessee in 1940 as one of many children in a poor family. As a young child she had double pneumonia, scarlet fever and polio, which left her with a weakened leg, and doctors expected she would never walk normally. Through years of therapy and determination she walked without a brace and began playing basketball, then running. She became a sprinter, and at the 1960 Rome Olympics she won three gold medals, earning a reputation as the fastest woman in the world. Dweck uses her story to show that athletes are not always 'naturals', and that ability can be built from very unpromising beginnings.

cards.t: Effort is not a sign of weakness
cards.b: A key difference between the mindsets is how they view effort. In the fixed mindset, Dweck explains, effort is for people without talent. Needing to try hard means you lack ability. So people avoid effort to protect their self-image, and some even avoid practicing so they have an excuse if they fail. In the growth mindset, effort is what makes you smart or talented. Dweck points to famous geniuses, such as Charles Darwin and Thomas Edison, whose achievements came through years of hard work, collaboration and failed experiments. She stresses that effort alone is not enough: people also need good strategies, help from others and the willingness to try new approaches when stuck.

Dweck examines business leaders. Some, like Lee Iacocca at Chrysler, she describes as showing a fixed mindset: surrounding themselves with admirers, taking credit, blaming others and focusing on their image. When things went wrong, they could not hear bad news. In contrast, Lou Gerstner at IBM and Anne Mulcahy at Xerox, both of whom rescued troubled companies, worked with teams, sought out problems, asked for feedback and focused on learning. Dweck also discusses Enron, arguing that its culture worshipped talent and made employees afraid to admit weakness. She calls the fixed-mindset leader's syndrome CEO disease: a need to look superior that undermines the organization.

Mindsets also shape relationships. In the fixed mindset, Dweck explains, people believe that qualities of a person, a partner or a relationship are fixed. If a relationship is meant to be, it should be effortless; problems reveal fundamental flaws. When conflict arises, people blame their partner's character or decide the relationship is doomed. In the growth mindset, people expect relationships to require work, communication and compromise. Problems are opportunities to understand each other better. Dweck also discusses rejection: people with a fixed mindset may feel judged and want revenge, while those with a growth mindset are more likely to want to understand what happened, forgive and move on.

Dweck argues that every word and action from a parent or teacher sends a message about mindset. Praising children for being smart or talented, however well-meant, tells them that ability is fixed and should be displayed. Labeling children as gifted can make them fear failure. Instead, she recommends praising the process: the effort, strategies, focus, persistence and improvement. Criticism should be constructive and focused on what to do next. When a child fails, adults should avoid both false reassurance and judgment, and instead help the child learn. She notes that children are quick to pick up the hidden messages in adults' reactions, such as disappointment at mistakes.

Dweck describes teachers who achieved remarkable results by believing all their students could grow. Marva Collins, a Chicago teacher, took children who had been labeled failures and, with high standards, love and hard work, had them reading classic literature. Jaime Escalante, at Garfield High School in East Los Angeles, taught calculus to students from poor families, and in 1982 so many passed the Advanced Placement exam that testers suspected cheating; most passed again on a retest. Dweck also describes Dorothy DeLay, a Juilliard violin teacher who believed talent could be developed, in contrast to colleagues who taught only students they saw as gifted.

cards.t: Teaching that the brain can grow
cards.b: Dweck and colleagues, including Lisa Blackwell, studied junior high school students in New York City. In one study, students attended a workshop of eight sessions. Half learned study skills only; the other half also learned that the brain is like a muscle that gets stronger with use, and that learning forms new connections between neurons. The math grades of the students taught the growth message improved, while the control group's grades continued to decline. Teachers, who did not know which group students were in, noticed changes in motivation. Dweck later developed an online program called Brainology based on these ideas, to teach students how their brains change with learning.

Dweck holds up John Wooden, the UCLA basketball coach who won ten national championships, as a model of growth-mindset leadership. Wooden did not demand that players win; he demanded full preparation and effort. He defined success as the peace of mind that comes from knowing you did your best to become the best you are capable of being. Dweck notes that he took responsibility for his teams' performance, focused on fundamentals and development, and treated every player with respect. Wooden believed character mattered more than talent and that players could improve through work. Dweck sees in him proof that a growth mindset can produce extraordinary results.

Dweck argues that mindsets can change, but it requires more than knowing about them. She recommends learning to hear your fixed-mindset voice, the one that says 'What if you fail?' or 'You're not a natural'. Recognize it as a voice, not the truth, and talk back with a growth-mindset response. In later editions, she suggests even giving your fixed-mindset persona a name, to notice what triggers it, such as criticism, deadlines or someone more successful. She also emphasizes that changing mindset is a journey: everyone has some fixed-mindset triggers, and the goal is not to eliminate them, but to recognize them and choose growth more often.

As the idea spread, Dweck noticed it being misunderstood, and in the 2016 edition she described a false growth mindset. Some people claimed a growth mindset simply because they were open-minded or optimistic. Some teachers praised effort even when it was not producing learning, which could leave struggling students feeling consoled but stuck. Others told children they could do anything without giving them the strategies and support to improve. Dweck stresses that a growth mindset is about learning: effort matters because it leads to progress, and when it does not, students need new strategies and help. Praising unproductive effort, she argues, is just as harmful as praising intelligence.

cards.q: Becoming is better than being: what matters is who you are growing into, not who you already are.
cards.b: This is a paraphrase of an idea Dweck uses to sum up the growth mindset, not her exact words. It contrasts the fixed mindset's need to prove a finished self with the growth mindset's commitment to developing.
