Mindset became hugely popular in schools, but later research has tempered its claims. A 2018 meta-analysis by Victoria Sisk and colleagues found that mindset interventions had, on average, very small effects on academic achievement. A large 2019 national study led by David Yeager, with Dweck as a co-author, found a modest but real benefit, mostly for lower-achieving students in supportive schools. The idea seems to help some students in some contexts, not to transform learning everywhere.

Critics also note that the book's examples, such as McEnroe and Jordan, or Iacocca and Gerstner, are interpretations of public figures rather than tested evidence, and that sorting people into mindsets after the fact risks circular reasoning. Some educators found that slogans like 'praise effort' were applied mechanically, which Dweck herself warned against. The core research holds up best when read as one influence on motivation, not a master key to success.

The Mueller and Dweck study shows that praising intelligence can make children avoid challenges. When someone does well, praise their effort, strategy, focus or improvement, such as 'You tried several approaches until one worked', rather than calling them smart. Do the same with colleagues and yourself. It reinforces the behaviors that lead to growth rather than a fragile label.

In a growth mindset, failure means you have not mastered something yet. When you or someone else says 'I can't do this' or 'I'm not good at math', add the word 'yet'. This small change reframes the statement from a verdict into a stage of learning, and opens the question of what to try next.

Dweck suggests recognizing the voice that says you will fail or look foolish. Notice when it appears, such as before a presentation or after criticism, and give it a name. Then answer it: 'This is hard, but I can learn it.' Seeing the voice as a reaction, not the truth, gives you room to choose growth.

The Columbia brain study showed fixed-mindset people ignoring the information that could help them. After a test, a review or a mistake, look past whether you were right or wrong and focus on what the feedback teaches. Ask people you trust for specific suggestions, and treat criticism as a tool rather than an attack.

Fixed-mindset children chose easy puzzles to look smart. Pick one area of your life where you have been avoiding difficulty, such as a skill you assume you lack, and choose a task slightly beyond your current ability. Expect to struggle, use good strategies, ask for help and judge yourself by what you learn.

Dweck warns that effort alone is not a growth mindset. If you have worked hard on something without improving, do not just push harder. Step back and try a new approach: a different method, a teacher, a smaller goal or feedback from someone more experienced. Growth comes from effort plus learning, not from effort by itself.

Think of an area of your life where you have decided you are simply 'not that kind of person', not creative, not athletic, not good with numbers. Where did that belief come from? What would you try if you believed it could change, and what is one small step you could take this week?

label: Book 19
title: The Innovator's Dilemma
subtitle: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail
author: Clayton M. Christensen

cards.b: If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Great companies fail by doing everything right
pts.d: listening to their best customers and chasing higher margins blinds them to disruptive technologies.

pts.h: Disruption starts small, cheap and worse
pts.d: like smaller disk drives, it wins fringe customers, then improves fast enough to take the mainstream.

pts.h: Incumbents flee upmarket, and it feels like winning
pts.d: steel mills happily handed minimills the low end until little was left.

pts.h: The cure is a separate, small, patient unit
pts.d: give the new technology to an organization whose customers need it, as Quantum and Kresge did.

cards.b: The Innovator's Dilemma asks a disturbing question: why do well-run, leading companies, with smart managers, deep pockets and loyal customers, so often lose their markets to small upstarts? Clayton Christensen, a Harvard Business School professor, argues that they are not lazy, arrogant or technically behind. They fail precisely because they follow the rules of good management: they listen closely to their best customers, invest in what promises the highest returns, and ignore small markets. Those habits are exactly right for most innovations, and fatal for one particular kind, which he calls disruptive technology. The dilemma is that the same sound decisions that build a great company can later destroy it.

Christensen's frame is deliberately uncomfortable. Most business books explain failure with villains: bureaucracy, complacency, poor planning. His evidence points elsewhere. The firms he studies saw the new technologies coming, often built them first, and then rationally decided not to pursue them because their customers did not want them and the profits looked thin. The rest of the book does two things. First, it builds a theory of when listening to customers leads you astray, drawn from decades of data on disk drives, excavators, steel and retailing. Second, it offers managers a set of rules for harnessing disruption instead of being destroyed by it, mostly by changing where and how the new venture is organized.

The book's central distinction is between two kinds of innovation. Sustaining technologies improve products along the dimensions that mainstream customers already value: faster, bigger, more reliable. Some are incremental and some are radical breakthroughs, but leading firms almost always win them, because their customers are asking for exactly that. Disruptive technologies are different. At first they perform worse on those familiar measures, yet they bring something else: they are usually simpler, cheaper, smaller or more convenient. Mainstream customers reject them, so they take root in small, low-margin or brand-new markets. The danger is that disruptive products then improve quickly, until they are good enough for the mainstream and come with the advantages the incumbent never matched.

To test his ideas, Christensen chose the computer disk drive industry, which he compared to the fruit flies geneticists study: generations come and go so quickly that you can watch evolution in years rather than decades. He assembled detailed data on almost every drive model and maker from the industry's early years into the 1990s. The pattern was striking. Established firms led nearly every sustaining improvement, including expensive, risky leaps such as new kinds of recording heads that demanded entirely new skills. Technical difficulty did not topple them. What did was a series of humbler shifts to physically smaller drives, which were technologically simple and yet repeatedly swept away the industry's leaders.

cards.t: Each smaller drive, a new set of winners
cards.b: In the 1970s, mainframe computers used 14-inch drives. When 8-inch drives appeared, they held less data and cost more per megabyte, so mainframe makers had no use for them. They found buyers instead among makers of minicomputers, a new and smaller market. The 14-inch leaders, listening to their mainframe customers, mostly stayed put; by the time 8-inch drives were good enough for mainframes, newcomers dominated. The same thing happened again with 5.25-inch drives for desktop PCs, 3.5-inch drives for portables, and the smaller sizes that followed. At each step, the new architecture was dismissed by the leaders' customers, flourished in an emerging market, and then moved up to take over the old one.

Why could firms master hard technologies but stumble on easy ones? Christensen's answer is the value network: the web of customers, suppliers and partners within which a company competes, and which defines what counts as good performance and acceptable profit. A mainframe-drive maker lives in a world where capacity is everything and margins are high; a portable-computer maker cares about size, weight, ruggedness and power use. A company's cost structure, sales force and sense of what a worthwhile opportunity looks like are all shaped by its network. A technology that is valuable in one network can look worthless in another. So firms fail not for lack of engineering, but because the new technology belongs to a network they are not in.

Seagate Technology had led the shift to 5.25-inch drives for desktop computers. By the mid-1980s its engineers had built working 3.5-inch prototypes. Marketing showed them to Seagate's main customers, the desktop PC makers, who saw little point: the smaller drives held less and cost more per megabyte, and desktops had plenty of room. Weighed against new high-capacity models those customers were asking for, the 3.5-inch project lost the internal contest for money and was shelved. Some of the engineers left and joined or founded startups, notably Conner Peripherals, which sold small drives to the emerging makers of portable computers. Seagate eventually joined the 3.5-inch market, but late, and mostly selling to its old desktop customers.

cards.t: When progress outruns what customers need
cards.b: Christensen's most important diagram shows two lines. One is the performance that customers in a market can actually use, which rises slowly. The other is the performance that technology delivers, which often rises much faster, because firms keep racing each other to satisfy their most demanding buyers. Eventually the technology overshoots what most customers need. That is the opening for disruption. A product that started out inadequate improves along its own steep path and crosses the line where it becomes good enough. Once mainstream customers no longer need more performance, they start choosing on other grounds, such as price, simplicity, size or convenience, exactly where the disruptive product is strongest.

cards.t: Cable shovels and the hydraulic backhoe
cards.b: Christensen shows the pattern is not just about electronics. For decades, mechanical excavators used steel cables pulled by winches, and a group of established manufacturers sold large cable shovels to contractors doing big earthmoving and mining jobs. After World War II, hydraulic excavators appeared. Early models were small and weak, with tiny buckets, often mounted on tractors, and useless for the big contractors. But they were ideal for small builders digging narrow trenches for water and sewer lines, a market the cable makers barely served. Hydraulic machines improved steadily until they could handle the big jobs too. By then newer firms led the industry, and most of the cable-shovel makers had disappeared.

The first of Christensen's principles is resource dependence: although managers think they decide where their company goes, in practice customers and investors do. A firm survives by giving its customers what they want and its investors the returns they expect, and it builds systems that kill ideas which fail that test. Those systems are healthy; they stop the company wasting money. But they also mean that a disruptive project, which current customers don't want and which promises low margins, will be starved of resources no matter what the chief executive says. The lesson is not that managers are powerless. It is that they must place disruptive projects where the customers who do want them can pull them forward.

cards.t: How Intel slipped out of memory
cards.b: Intel was founded on memory chips, and in its early years DRAMs were its core business. In the late 1970s and early 1980s it also began making microprocessors. As Japanese competitors drove DRAM prices down, Intel's middle managers kept following a simple rule: allocate scarce manufacturing capacity to products that earn the highest margin per wafer. Microprocessors kept winning. Christensen, drawing on research by Robert Burgelman, shows that by the time senior executives formally decided to leave the DRAM business in the mid-1980s, the company's everyday resource-allocation process had already shifted most of its capacity away. Here the same mechanism that blocks disruptive projects worked in Intel's favor, moving it toward the more profitable market.

cards.t: Small markets can't feed big companies
cards.b: The second principle is about scale. A company with five billion dollars in revenue that wants to grow 20 percent a year needs a billion dollars in new sales every year. Disruptive technologies, by definition, begin in small markets worth a few million. To a large firm, those markets cannot move the needle, so it rationally waits until they are big enough to matter. But by then the early entrants have learned the market and built their positions. Christensen argues that success makes this worse: the larger and more successful a company becomes, the harder it is for it to take emerging markets seriously, even when it can see them clearly.

cards.t: The Newton that was too small
cards.b: Apple's Newton, an early handheld computer launched in 1993, became a byword for failure. Christensen offers a different reading. In its first couple of years the Newton actually sold more units than the Apple II had in its own early years, and the Apple II had launched a great company. The difference was Apple's size. A small startup in the late 1970s could thrive on modest sales and learn as it went. The Apple of the 1990s was a large firm that needed a huge, immediate market to justify its investment, so it made big forecasts and big promises the product could not meet. Measured against a big company's needs, a promising beginning looked like a flop.

cards.t: Markets that don't exist can't be analyzed
cards.b: The third principle is that you cannot do market research on markets that do not yet exist. For sustaining innovations, analysts can measure demand, survey customers and forecast sales with reasonable confidence. For disruptive ones, the eventual customers and uses are usually unknown, even to the customers themselves. Christensen notes that forecasts for disruptive products are almost always badly wrong. Managers trained to demand numbers and detailed plans therefore either refuse to invest or commit heavily to a guess. His alternative is what he calls discovery-based, or agnostic, marketing: assume your forecast is wrong, spend little, plan to learn, and be ready to change course quickly as the real market reveals itself.

When Honda entered the American motorcycle market in 1959, its plan was to sell large touring bikes to compete with Harley-Davidson and the British makers. It went badly: the bikes broke down and leaked oil when ridden hard over long distances. Meanwhile, the small team in Los Angeles was zipping around on Honda's little 50cc Supercubs to run errands. People kept asking where they could buy one, including for off-road fun in the hills. Honda reluctantly began selling the small bikes, often through sporting-goods stores rather than motorcycle dealers, and found a huge market of people who had never wanted a big motorcycle at all. The winning strategy emerged from accident, not planning.

The fourth principle is that an organization's capabilities define its disabilities. Christensen later framed a company's capabilities as three things: its resources, such as people, money and technology; its processes, the routines by which it turns those into products; and its values, the criteria by which it decides what is worth doing, such as which margins and order sizes are attractive. Resources can move, but processes and values are built to serve a particular business, and they work well there. In a disruptive market they misfire. A company whose values say that only large, high-margin orders matter will find it can't get excited about a small, cheap product, however talented its people are.

From the 1960s, minimills, which melt scrap steel in electric arc furnaces, began making steel far more cheaply than the big integrated mills, but at first the quality was poor. The only product they could make was concrete reinforcing bar, rebar, the lowest-margin corner of the market. The integrated mills were glad to give it up and saw their margins rise. Then the minimills improved and moved up to bars and rods, then to structural beams, each time pushing the integrated mills out of a low-margin segment they were happy to leave. Finally, in the late 1980s, Nucor used thin-slab casting to enter sheet steel, the integrated mills' most profitable stronghold.

cards.t: The easy road up, the hard road down
cards.b: The minimill story shows why the attack is so hard to resist. Christensen calls it an asymmetry of motivation. Moving upmarket into higher-margin products is attractive: it raises profits and pleases investors, and every company's ambitious managers want to do it. Moving downmarket into cheaper products with lower margins looks like madness, because it hurts profits and requires cutting costs the company has spent years building. So as entrants attack from below, incumbents retreat upward and feel good about it, with rising margins and happier shareholders. They do not notice they are being squeezed into a smaller corner of the market until there is nowhere left to go.

cards.t: Quantum, Kresge and the separate unit
cards.b: Christensen found that the few incumbents that succeeded with disruptive technology did it by creating independent organizations. Quantum, a maker of 8-inch drives, saw the 3.5-inch opportunity in the mid-1980s and backed a separate company, Plus Development, which built a small drive that slotted into IBM-compatible PCs. As Quantum's old business faded, the new unit's products kept the company alive. In retailing, S.S. Kresge launched its discount chain Kmart as a separate operation and transformed itself, while Woolworth tried to run its discount chain, Woolco, inside its existing variety-store organization and failed. The lesson: a disruptive business needs its own cost structure and its own idea of what a good order is.

The fifth principle is that technology supply may not match market demand, and Christensen describes how the basis of competition shifts as products overshoot. He borrows a buying hierarchy: customers first choose on functionality. Once several products meet their needs, they choose on reliability. When those are reliable enough, they choose on convenience, and finally on price. Each shift moves the battlefield. A firm still competing on more features when customers have begun choosing on convenience or price is pouring money into something buyers no longer reward, which is exactly the moment when a simpler, cheaper, more convenient disruptive product finds its opening.

cards.t: Purer insulin, or an easier pen?
cards.b: In the early 1980s Eli Lilly introduced Humulin, human insulin made with recombinant DNA, after investing heavily. It was purer than the insulin from cows and pigs that diabetics had used. But animal insulin had already become pure enough for nearly all patients, so few would pay much of a premium for still more purity. Lilly had improved a dimension that had been oversupplied. Meanwhile, Novo, a Danish firm, focused on convenience, developing insulin pens that replaced fiddly syringes and vials. Patients and doctors valued that, and Novo grew fast. Christensen uses the story to show how competition shifts once a product is good enough on its original dimension.

cards.t: The electric car, as a test
cards.b: In the book's later chapters Christensen applies his framework to a live question of the 1990s: how should a carmaker handle electric vehicles? Electric cars then had short range, slow top speed and high costs, so measured against what mainstream drivers wanted they were clearly inferior, and regulatory mandates were forcing them on reluctant manufacturers. Christensen argues they look like a disruptive technology. Instead of trying to sell them to ordinary drivers, a company should set up a small, independent unit to find customers who would value what they did well: simplicity, low running costs, and short trips, perhaps for teenagers or city errands. Then it should improve them on that steeper trajectory.

cards.q: The very things that make a company excellent, listening to its best customers and investing where returns are highest, are what lead it to fail when a disruptive technology arrives.
cards.b: This is a paraphrase of the book's central idea, not Christensen's exact words. It captures why the dilemma is so hard: the failure does not come from bad managers making mistakes, but from good managers making the decisions they were trained to make.

In 2014 the historian Jill Lepore, writing in The New Yorker, argued that Christensen's evidence was more selective than it looked. Some firms he counted as defeated, she said, recovered or thrived later; Seagate, for instance, went on to become a leading drive maker. A 2015 study by Andrew King and Baljir Baatartogtokh examined cases cited as disruption and found that only a minority fit all of the theory's conditions. Christensen and his defenders replied that the theory was about mechanisms and probabilities, not iron laws, but the debate is a reminder to test the pattern against each new case.

The theory's success has blurred it. Disruption became a fashionable label for any startup that shakes up an industry, though Christensen insisted it meant something specific: entering at the low end or in a new market with an inferior, cheaper product. He himself argued that Uber, for instance, did not fit. The theory is also easier to apply after the fact than in advance; Christensen famously doubted the iPhone, which in fact entered at the top of its market. It explains a great deal, but it is not a crystal ball.

cards.t: Listen to the customers you don't have
cards.b: Seagate's desktop buyers told it, quite correctly, that they didn't need 3.5-inch drives. The mistake was treating them as the only voice that mattered. When you evaluate a new idea, ask not just whether your current customers want it, but who might want it badly, even if they are small, poor or unfamiliar to you today.

Ask whether your product is already better than most customers can use, as purer insulin was. If buyers stop paying for extra features and start choosing on convenience or price, the ground is shifting under you. That is the moment to invest in simplicity and ease, and to take the cheap, good-enough rival seriously rather than dismissing it.

cards.t: Give new ideas a home of their own
cards.b: Quantum's Plus Development and Kresge's Kmart worked because they were separate, with their own costs, customers and sense of a good order. If you are starting something genuinely different inside an established team or company, protect it from being judged by the old business's margins and priorities, or the resource-allocation process will quietly starve it.

cards.t: Match the size of the bet to the market
cards.b: The Newton shows what happens when a large organization needs a small new market to be big immediately. Start new ventures small enough that early wins feel like wins. A modest team that can get excited about a few thousand customers will learn faster, and survive longer, than a big one that needs millions to justify its existence.

Honda found its American market by accident, after its plan failed. In uncertain territory, treat your forecast as a hypothesis, not a promise. Spend little at first, run small experiments, watch what real customers actually do, and keep enough money and flexibility in reserve to change direction once the market shows you where it is.

cards.t: Be wary of the comfortable retreat
cards.b: The integrated steel mills felt better each time they gave up a low-margin product to the minimills. If you notice yourself happily abandoning the cheap end of your work, your career or your market because it is unprofitable, ask who is taking it, and whether they are getting better quickly. Today's rebar can become tomorrow's sheet steel.

Think of something you do well, at work or in life, that you are proud of improving year after year. Is there a cheaper, simpler or more convenient alternative that you have dismissed as not good enough? Who uses it, how fast is it getting better, and what would you do differently if you took it seriously today?
